faq.question: How do you mix 10 and 30 volume developer to make 20 volume?
faq.answer: To formulate 20 Volume (6%) developer, mix equal parts (1:1 ratio) of 10 Volume (3%) and 30 Volume (9%) developer. For example, 30ml of 10 Vol + 30ml of 30 Vol equals 60ml of 20 Vol developer.

faq.question: Can I mix different developer brands together?
faq.answer: No. Different manufacturers formulate developers with proprietary buffers, conditioning agents, and viscosity stabilizers. Blending different brands can cause emulsion breakdown or unpredictable lift.

faq.question: Can you dilute 40 volume developer with water to make 20 volume?
faq.answer: Never use water to dilute developer. Water dilutes the preservative system, alters the pH balance, and thins the product consistency, causing bleeding into foils or scalp irritation.

faq.question: How does the Alligation calculation formula work?
faq.answer: The formula uses Pearson's Square (Alligation Alternate): Parts Low = High Vol - Target Vol; Parts High = Target Vol - Low Vol. Total parts equal Parts Low + Parts High.

education.heading: The Chemistry of Developer Volume Blending (The Alligation Method)
intro: Behind the chair, hydrogen peroxide (H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) developers are the chemical oxidative drivers of permanent hair color, high-lift blonding, and toner deposit. The "Volume" rating denotes the volume of pure oxygen gas liberated from one volume of liquid developer during complete oxidation (for example, 20 Volume developer releases 20 times its volume in oxygen, representing approximately 6% hydrogen peroxide concentration by weight).

When a colorist runs out of 20 Volume mid-service, canceling appointments or estimating measurements compromises both lift and tonal deposit. Using the pharmaceutical Alligation Alternate method (the rule of mixtures), any two known developer concentrations from the same product line can be mathematically proportioned to create an exact intermediate strength without chemical guesswork.

walkthrough.title: The Exact Alligation Formula Walkthrough
steps: Step 1: Parts of Low Volume Needed = High Volume − Target Volume
Step 2: Parts of High Volume Needed = Target Volume − Low Volume
Step 3: Total Parts = Parts Low + Parts High
walkthrough.example:
Worked Example: Formulate 60ml of 20 Vol using 10 Vol and 30 Vol:
• Parts of 10 Vol = 30 − 20 = 10 parts
• Parts of 30 Vol = 20 − 10 = 10 parts
• Total Parts = 20 parts → Ratio is 10:10 (1:1 equal parts) → 30ml of 10 Vol + 30ml of 30 Vol = 60ml of 20 Vol.

education.rules_heading: Critical Station Rules for Mixing Developers

rules.title: Stay Within the Same Brand & Product Line
rules.body: Never cross-mix developers from different manufacturers (e.g. Wella with Redken). Manufacturers formulate with distinct lipid carriers, viscosity thickeners, and proprietary buffering agents that can destabilize when combined.

rules.title: Measure by Digital Weight (Grams or Ounces)
rules.body: Measuring by eyeball or cup lines introduces 10%–20% volumetric error. Always tare your mixing bowl on a 0.1g digital scale for exact formulation repeatability.

rules.title: Never Dilute Developer with Tap Water
rules.body: Adding tap water dilutes the preservative system, alters the pH balance, and causes emulsion thinning, leading to packet bleed and patchy lift. Always blend with a lower volume developer.

education.heading: Understanding the Color Wheel Rule
intro: Every time hair is lightened, it passes through a predictable sequence of underlying pigments — warm red at the darkest levels, through orange, into yellow and pale yellow at the lightest levels. This is the "exposed pigment" you are working against whenever you tone.

To neutralize an unwanted warm tone, you apply the complementary (opposite) color from the color wheel. The chart below maps each of the ten standard levels of lift to its exposed pigment and the complementary toner family that cancels it out.

walkthrough.title: How to read the chart
steps: Identify the level of lift you have reached (or are aiming for) after lightening — Level 1 is black, Level 10 is the lightest pale yellow/white.
Find that level's exposed undertone in the table — this is the warmth you will see in the hair.
Select a toner or color containing the matching neutralizer pigment shown alongside it.
Apply with a low-volume developer (typically 5–10 Vol) for a short processing time, since you are depositing tone rather than lifting further.
walkthrough.example: Example: hair has lifted to Level 7 and shows yellow-orange/gold-copper warmth. The color wheel calls for a blue-violet ash neutralizer — a toner in the .12 / .21 family — to cancel it.

rules.title: Green neutralizes Red
rules.body: Used at the darkest levels of lift (1–3), where the strongest warm/red pigment is exposed.

rules.title: Blue neutralizes Orange
rules.body: Used at mid-range levels of lift (5–6), as the exposed pigment shifts from red toward orange.

rules.title: Violet neutralizes Yellow
rules.body: Used at the lightest levels of lift (8–10), where the exposed pigment is yellow or pale yellow.

warnings: This chart is a formulation guide, not a guarantee — actual exposed warmth varies with hair porosity, prior chemical history, and the brand/line of color used.
Always perform a strand test before full application, especially on previously colored or chemically treated hair.
Follow your toner manufacturer's own developer volume and processing time directions — they take priority over the general guidance given here.
safety.manufacturer_note: Formulas use universal metric and imperial units compatible with major professional brands including Wella, Redken, Schwarzkopf, L'Oréal, and Guy Tang Mydentity, but exact pigment names and numbering vary by line — always cross-reference your own color system.

faq.q: What formula is used in this guide?
